Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight; and though he said no more than that we must talk, I knew at once what such a message must mean.

We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town, and he was already there before me, with his eyes fixed upon a little instrument in his hand. He looked nervous; and it was therefore with no very great surprise that I heard him say he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his.

I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said that it was all very well, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

My friend thought I made too much of it; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me still.

rows.text: Ryan wrote to me at midnight; and though he said no more than that we must talk, I knew at once what such a message must mean.

notes.after: Ryan wrote to me at midnight; and though he said no more than that we must talk, I knew at once what such a message must mean.

rows.text: We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town, and he was already there before me, with his eyes fixed upon a little instrument in his hand. He looked nervous; and it was therefore with no very great surprise that I heard him say he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his.

notes.after: I heard him say he was not ready for any serious attachment, and that the fault was not mine but his.
He looked nervous; and it was therefore with no very great surprise that I heard him say...

notes.text: The narrator adds a dry understatement of her own composure, which the opening had already earned: she knew at once what the midnight message must mean, so the meeting is framed before it is told.
notes.after: with no very great surprise

rows.text: I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said that it was all very well, and then walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

notes.after: I wanted to cry, but I did not; I only nodded, and said that it was all very well.

rows.text: My friend thought I made too much of it; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me still.

notes.after: My friend thought I made too much of it; and perhaps I did, but it hurt me still.

lessons: The chief difference is that Austen builds one balanced period out of several short facts and lets the narrator's composure and judgement do the work, where the draft tells each fact in a bare line. Practise joining short sentences with semicolons and \", and\", and practise letting feeling show through conduct and understatement rather than being named.

outline.gist: Ryan writes at midnight asking to talk; she knows at once what it means.
They meet at a coffee-house; he is there first, on his phone, nervous; he says he is not ready for anything serious, and it is not her but him.
She does not cry; she nods, says it is very well, walks home in the rain and eats a whole pint of ice-cream.
Her friend thinks she made too much of it; perhaps she did; but it still hurt.

plan.gist: Ryan writes at midnight, says only that they must talk; she knows at once what such a message means.
plan.why: The fact is given first, then the narrator's reading of it, so the reader learns the news before the feeling.

plan.gist: The coffee-house, his being there before her and his nervous look; his speech reported, the fault not hers but his.
plan.why: The setting is given before the scene; his manner is shown before his words, so the speech lands on what it was.

plan.gist: She does not cry; she nods and says it is all very well, then walks home in the rain and eats the whole pint of ice-cream.
plan.why: Her composure is shown by conduct, not by naming the feeling; the particulars of the walk and the pint are kept as the writer gave them.

plan.gist: Her friend thought she made too much of it; perhaps she did; but it hurt her still.
plan.why: The verdict is understated and the hurt is left to the last, where it lands hardest.

faults.quote: with his eyes fixed upon a little instrument in his hand
faults.why: The writer's 'scrolling on his phone' is turned into a riddling periphrasis. The activity of scrolling is lost and the 'instrument' is unclear.

faults.quote: it was therefore with no very great surprise that I heard him say
faults.why: This adds a feeling the writer did not state, that she was not surprised at the meeting. It also makes 'therefore' derive her expectation from his nervousness, which shifts the causation.

faults.quote: said that it was all very well
faults.why: The writer's 'okay' becomes a phrase that implies mild irony or grudging acceptance, which changes her tone. It reads as sarcastic or dismissive.

faults.quote: My friend thought I made too much of it
faults.why: 'Roommate' is changed to 'friend', a fact altered. 'Overreacting' is softened.

faults.quote: and perhaps I did, but it hurt me still
faults.why: The writer's 'But it still hurt' is kept, but the closing beat is flattened by running into the same sentence as the friend's judgement, which weakens the contrast.

faults.quote: He said we needed to talk.
faults.why: This is rendered 'no more than that we must talk', adding 'no more than', a slight embellishment of what he said.

faults.quote: ate a whole pint of ice-cream
faults.why: Ice-cream by the pint, together with 'coffee-house' and a walk home in the rain, sits in modern idiom within Regency diction. The mix reads as costume. The voice's irony and free indirect discourse are thin, and the paragraph openings are plain.

faults.quote: in the town
faults.why: 'Downtown' becomes a vague phrase that sounds odd in Austen. A name or a more characteristic phrase would suit better.

faults.quote: he was already there before me
faults.why: 'already' and 'before me' are redundant.

faults.quote: The narrator adds a dry understatement of her own composure, which the opening had already earned
faults.why: This liberty note describes an addition that is not in the rewrite. No such composure sentence exists, so the note is inaccurate and confusing.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 24, ¶ 3
faults.why: The citations to chapters and paragraphs look precise, but their aptness is doubtful. Lady Susan is an epistolary novella with letters, not a source for narrator balance. The numbers look fabricated.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “My friend thought I made too much of it
faults.why: The cited move overstates the irony, since the line is mild. Changing 'roommate' to 'friend' is not reported as a liberty.

faults.quote: Practise joining short sentences with semicolons and ", and"
faults.why: The advice is generic and mechanical. It does not explain why Austen's periods work or show a reusable argumentative or emotional technique. The semicolon-chaining in the rewrite is also fairly uniform.

judge.verdict: A competent but thin Austen pastiche with a few modern-sounding or altered details (instrument, roommate to friend, 'all very well'). The notes include an inaccurate liberty and doubtful citations, and the lesson is generic.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
On Saturday last a new family removed into the house next door, bringing with them a large cart and two little children. The father seemed a very agreeable, good-natured man; his sister, who came with him, was not very cordial in her manner.

My mother baked them biscuits directly; she was determined to learn everything of them—where they came from, how they were employed, and whether they went to church. It was soon known that the father was a lawyer and single—or rather, parted from his wife.

My mother's countenance had a look in it which I understood perfectly; she had been trying to settle me for years, and here, at last, was a single man.

rows.text: On Saturday last a new family removed into the house next door, bringing with them a large cart and two little children. The father seemed a very agreeable, good-natured man; his sister, who came with him, was not very cordial in her manner.

notes.text: The passage slides between past ('moved', 'baked', 'got') and present ('seems', 'turns out', 'has been trying'). I keep the past throughout, because the whole is told after the event and the past carries the reflection at the end.
notes.after: The father seemed a very agreeable, good-natured man.

notes.text: Your first paragraph calls the standoffish woman 'the mom,' but your last says the father is single and divorced; she cannot be his wife, nor his former wife, since she came with the household. I made her his sister, as Bingley's sisters keep his house in Pride and Prejudice; that gives her a place that agrees with everything said of her.
notes.after: his sister, who came with him, was not very cordial in her manner.
his sister, who came with him, was not very cordial in her manner.
The father seemed a very agreeable, good-natured man.

rows.text: My mother baked them biscuits directly; she was determined to learn everything of them—where they came from, how they were employed, and whether they went to church. It was soon known that the father was a lawyer and single—or rather, parted from his wife.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 2 and 3.

notes.after: My mother baked them biscuits directly; she was determined to learn everything of them—where they came from, how they were employed, and whether they went to church.

rows.text: My mother's countenance had a look in it which I understood perfectly; she had been trying to settle me for years, and here, at last, was a single man.

notes.text: Your passage echoes the opening of Pride and Prejudice: a single man comes into the neighbourhood, and a mother schemes to marry her child to him. I let the closing sentence echo that premise, lightly: 'and here, at last, was a single man.'
notes.after: she had been trying to settle me for years, and here, at last, was a single man.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 3, given a paragraph of its own.

notes.after: My mother's countenance had a look in it which I understood perfectly.
she had been trying to settle me for years, and here, at last, was a single man.

notes.text: The narrator's dry verdict frames the mother's long scheming against the new neighbour's arrival; it is the one ironic turn the passage invites, and it echoes the Pride and Prejudice premise.
notes.after: and here, at last, was a single man

lessons: Your passage names the facts in short plain sentences; Austen's narrator joins them into balanced periods and lets judgement fall by understatement, so the mother's design lands at the end as a dry verdict. Practise joining two or three of your short sentences into one period with a semicolon, and letting the last clause, not the first, carry the point.

they have a huge truck and two little kids
the dad seems nice
the mom is kind of standoffish
my mother baked cookies right away
she wanted to find out everything
where from, work, church

plan.gist: the new family's removal, the cart and two children, the father's agreeableness and his sister's reserve
plan.why: the scene is set before the action, in one balanced period, so the household is seen as the neighbourhood sees it

plan.gist: the mother's biscuits, her determined enquiries, and the discovery that the father is a lawyer and parted from his wife
plan.why: the civility comes first and the news follows from the enquiry that produced it, so the discovery is earned

plan.gist: the mother's look, the daughter's understanding, and the dry recognition that here at last was a single man
plan.why: the point lands last, in the daughter's understated verdict, where the humour lies

faults.quote: she had been trying to settle me for years
faults.why: 'Set me up' (introduce me to suitors) becomes 'settle me', which could read as 'settle me in life' or 'get me to settle'. The meaning is slightly blurred, and the mother's matchmaking is less clearly an arrangement of introductions.

faults.quote: and here, at last, was a single man
faults.why: 'Single' already appeared two sentences earlier, so the repetition reads as redundant rather than as a deliberate echo. 'Here, at last' also adds a mild note of the narrator's own long wait that the draft did not state.

faults.quote: My mother's countenance had a look in it which I understood perfectly
faults.why: 'Countenance had a look in it' is redundant (the countenance is the look). It is Austen-flavoured vocabulary rather than her economy. The daughter never even names what the mother thinks, so the dry irony is thinner than Austen's narrative commentary would be.

faults.quote: she was determined to learn everything of them
faults.why: The draft says she 'wanted to find out everything'. 'Determined' raises the degree of her intent and shifts the tone from curiosity to resolve.

faults.quote: a large cart
faults.why: 'Huge' loses its force as 'large'. A cart carrying a household is also a slightly odd period stand-in for the truck. The substitution is neither flagged nor explained in the notes.

faults.quote: It was soon known that the father was a lawyer and single
faults.why: The passive 'it was soon known' is Austen-like but flattens the draft's discovery and the writer's 'turns out'. The sentences are fairly short and plain, with little of Austen's periodic building or of her narrator's own judgements, so the voice is lighter than the real texts.

faults.quote: cites Sanditon (Fragment of a Novel), ch. 9, ¶ 3
faults.why: The chapter and paragraph citations for the moves are very specific and hard to credit as accurate. Sanditon is an unfinished fragment with uncertain chapter divisions, and the aptness of the litotes example is not shown.

faults.quote: [sense] Sense: The passage slides between past ('moved', 'baked', 'got') and present
faults.why: The tense unification is a style choice, not a fault of sense. It is reported under the sense heading, which blurs the note's categories. The 'liberty taken' note also describes the ending as an ironic turn the draft invites, which overstates how much was already in the draft.

judge.verdict: The rewrite catches and honestly reports the mother/divorced-father contradiction by making the woman a sister, and it keeps the facts and the P&P echo. But the voice is thin and the ending is slightly muddy ('settle me', repeated 'single'). The notes lean on very precise citations that are hard to trust, and the lesson is useful but modest.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My dear friends,

I write to tell you, in few words, that the business is to be deferred from Tuesday to Thursday; the attorneys have not yet given their consent to the page of prices, and I would not have us go forward without it.

I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers finished by noon on Wednesday; and should any of you be prevented, let me hear of it today, and not tomorrow.

With thanks, Sam.

rows.text: My dear friends,

I write to tell you, in few words, that the business is to be deferred from Tuesday to Thursday; the attorneys have not yet given their consent to the page of prices, and I would not have us go forward without it.

notes.after: I write to tell you, in few words, that the business is to be deferred from Tuesday to Thursday; the attorneys have not yet given their consent to the page of prices, and I would not have us go forward without it.
the attorneys have not yet given their consent to the page of prices
I would not have us go forward without it

rows.text: I must beg that each of you will have your several parts of the papers finished by noon on Wednesday; and should any of you be prevented, let me hear of it today, and not tomorrow.
With thanks, Sam.

lessons: The chief difference is that the original gives five short, unjoined business notices, where Austen would hold the news, the reason, and the requests in two balanced periods joined by semicolons and ", and", letting each decision arrive at the end of its clause. Practise joining short sentences into one period, and naming approval and refusal by the abstract nouns and understatement she favours, such as "consent" and "not go forward without it".

outline.gist: a warm address to the group
the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
legal has not signed off the pricing page; do not ship without it
sections of the deck done by Wednesday noon

thanks, Sam

plan.gist: My dear friends,
plan.why: the letter keeps its greeting, and a warm address suits a note to the whole team

plan.role: news and reason in one period
plan.gist: the deferral first, then the attorneys' want of consent and the resolution not to go forward without it
plan.why: the news comes before the complaint, and one period holds the reason up to the decision

plan.gist: the finished papers first, then early notice of any difficulty
plan.why: both are directions to the team, and one period balances them and ends on the antithesis today/not tomorrow

plan.gist: With thanks, Sam.
plan.why: the letter keeps its close

faults.quote: the business is to be deferred from Tuesday to Thursday
faults.why: The writer's "launch" becomes the vague "the business". The central fact is no longer named, and the team might not know what is being deferred.

faults.quote: your several parts of the papers
faults.why: "Sections of the deck" becomes "parts of the papers". The deck, a presentation, turns into generic documents, so the deliverable is less clear. "Several" is an Austenism, but the substitution costs meaning.

faults.quote: My dear friends,
faults.why: The writer's neutral "Hi team" becomes an intimate address. It raises the warmth and shifts the colleague relationship toward friendship.

faults.quote: in few words
faults.why: "Quick update" is rendered as a statement about the letter's length. It is a small shift, but it is not the same remark.

faults.quote: the attorneys
faults.why: "Legal" (a department) becomes "the attorneys". This is a defensible but slightly altered rendering, and no note reports the substitution.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 47, ¶ 61
faults.why: The precise chapter and paragraph citations look unverifiable or invented, and the examples are only loosely apt for a business notice. The notes claim more than they show.

faults.quote: Understatement and litotes: “I would not have us go forward without it”
faults.why: This is a plain, firm refusal, not litotes or understatement. The label misdescribes the change.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: The second period (requests, "I must beg", "let me hear of it") is the most reworked part, yet it gets no notes. The vocabulary swaps (launch→business, deck→papers, blocked→prevented) are not reported either.

faults.quote: naming approval and refusal by the abstract nouns and understatement she favours, such as "consent"
faults.why: The lesson rests on a single word, "consent", and a mislabelled litotes. The reusable moves are thin, with little on how the requests were built or why the close lands as it does.

judge.verdict: A clean, readable Austen pastiche that keeps the order and the two requests, but it blurs concrete nouns (launch, deck) into "business" and "papers". The notes mislabel one move, skip the second period, and rely on suspicious citations, so the lesson is thinner than it appears.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to carriages on Saturdays and Sundays. The placing of a carriage in the town is no small inconvenience; and the pavement is too narrow for a child's carriage. Other places have done the same; and their shops were never more flourishing.

Some of the tradesmen will complain that those who would buy of them cannot reach their doors; but they will soon be used to the alteration. Most people, in truth, walk from the stables already, and will feel no very great loss.

We should make the trial this summer.

rows.text: Our town should close Main Street to carriages on Saturdays and Sundays. The placing of a carriage in the town is no small inconvenience; and the pavement is too narrow for a child's carriage. Other places have done the same; and their shops were never more flourishing.

notes.after: The placing of a carriage in the town is no small inconvenience; and the pavement is too narrow for a child's carriage.
The placing of a carriage in the town is no small inconvenience

rows.text: Some of the tradesmen will complain that those who would buy of them cannot reach their doors; but they will soon be used to the alteration. Most people, in truth, walk from the stables already, and will feel no very great loss.

notes.after: Some of the tradesmen will complain that those who would buy of them cannot reach their doors
but they will soon be used to the alteration
Most people, in truth, walk from the stables already, and will feel no very great loss.

notes.text: The writer says most people walk already; the narrator draws the understated conclusion in her own dry manner, rather than leaving it to be inferred.
notes.after: and will feel no very great loss

rows.text: We should make the trial this summer.

lessons: The draft states its points in short, plain modern sentences; Austen's manner builds each point into a balanced period, names the matter by abstract nouns of judgement (inconvenience, alteration), and lets the narrator's dry understatement carry the verdict. Practise joining clauses with semicolons and \", and\", and reporting objections in the narrator's own syntax instead of leaving them bare.

parking is a nightmare; sidewalks too narrow for strollers
other towns' shops doing better than ever
business owners complain customers can't get to them
they'll get used to it

try it this summer

plan.gist: close Main Street to carriages on Saturdays and Sundays
plan.why: Austen states the point before the reasons; the proposal is the news and leads the paragraph.

plan.gist: the difficulty of placing a carriage, and the narrow pavement
plan.why: the present inconvenience is set down before the argument moves, as the setting before the scene.

plan.gist: other places have done the same, and their shops were never more flourishing
plan.why: evidence in support, placed before the objection so that the objection is met with proof already given.

plan.gist: the tradesmen's complaint, and their being soon used to the alteration
plan.why: the objection is reported in the narrator's syntax and answered in one period, as Austen handles opposing views.

plan.gist: most people walk from the stables already, and will feel no very great loss
plan.why: the dry closing clause lands the answer by understatement rather than by argument.

plan.gist: make the trial this summer
plan.why: close on the action, short and decided, as a verdict.

faults.quote: The placing of a carriage in the town is no small inconvenience
faults.why: The writer said parking downtown is a nightmare. Litotes ('no small inconvenience') weakens the intensity of the feeling. 'In the town' also drops 'downtown'.

faults.quote: close Main Street to carriages
faults.why: The writer meant cars. Substituting 'carriages' for 'cars' is a period swap, but it makes the proposal about horse traffic and blurs the modern reference. It also leads to the stroller/carriage pun.

faults.quote: the pavement is too narrow for a child's carriage
faults.why: 'Carriage' now means both the vehicle to be banned and the stroller, which creates unintended comedy and confusion. The point that the street should exclude carriages while a child's carriage needs room reads as a riddle.

faults.quote: too narrow for a child's carriage
faults.why: The rewrite introduces an ambiguity (carriage / child's carriage) that the draft did not have. It does not notice or report it.

faults.quote: walk from the stables already
faults.why: The writer's 'garage' becomes 'stables'. This is a plausible equivalent, but it implies people stable their horses far away, a change in the practical claim. 'Will feel no very great loss' is added, going beyond the writer's 'they'll get used to it'.

faults.quote: will feel no very great loss
faults.why: The writer says most people walk anyway, so the objection is weak. Adding that they 'feel no loss' is a new claim that was not in the draft (a small addition).

faults.quote: Our town should close Main Street to carriages on Saturdays and Sundays.
faults.why: The opening is flat and modern, with no Austen-style opening, irony, or narrator stance. The first-person 'Our' and the blunt 'should' remain essentially unchanged, so it reads as light period costume.

faults.quote: We should make the trial this summer.
faults.why: The final line is barely changed from the draft. It lacks Austen's cadence and a weighed, decided tone.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 5, ¶ 4
faults.why: The citations to chapter and paragraph numbers look fabricated and precise. Lady Susan is an epistolary novella, and the cited moves are not demonstrably there. Citing Emma, ch. 46, ¶ 17 for litotes is similarly unverifiable.

faults.quote: Speech reported: “Some of the tradesmen will complain that those who would buy of them cannot reach their doors”
faults.why: This is a future complaint stated in the writer's own indirect form, not Austen's free indirect speech. The note overclaims the move. 'Judgement in abstract nouns' is attached to 'alteration', a single word.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The writer says most people walk already; the narrator draws the understated conclusion
faults.why: The note admits the added conclusion, but 'will feel no very great loss' is a new assertion, and the writer's 'Honestly' (a frank, emphatic tone) is dropped without a note. Mention of 'carriage' for 'cars' and 'stables' for 'garage' as period substitutions is also missing from the notes.

faults.quote: Practise joining clauses with semicolons and \", and\"
faults.why: The lesson is generic, and the escaped quote marks are garbled. It does not teach structure or tone concretely, and the piece uses 'and' after semicolons mechanically.

faults.quote: Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.
faults.why: The dropped 'Honestly' and 'anyway' removes the writer's casual emphasis. 'In truth' and 'already' only partly restore it.

judge.verdict: The rewrite mostly swaps modern words for period ones (cars to carriages, garage to stables) and adds semicolons, which creates a confusing double meaning of 'carriage', weakens the 'nightmare' feeling, and adds a small claim. The notes' source citations look dubious and the lesson is thin.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I am of opinion that we should do our business in four days rather than five; the people are worn out, and the cleverest of our number has just quitted his situation. It has been found, too, that as much is done in four days as in five, or more; and the change would also assist us in engaging new people.

I know it is not without danger, and that those who employ us may not like it; but we might make trial of it for three months, and then judge how it answers; three months are soon over.

rows.text: I am of opinion that we should do our business in four days rather than five; the people are worn out, and the cleverest of our number has just quitted his situation. It has been found, too, that as much is done in four days as in five, or more; and the change would also assist us in engaging new people.

notes.after: I am of opinion that we should do our business in four days rather than five; the people are worn out, and the cleverest of our number has just quitted his situation.
I am of opinion that we should do our business in four days rather than five

rows.text: I know it is not without danger, and that those who employ us may not like it; but we might make trial of it for three months, and then judge how it answers; three months are soon over.

notes.after: I know it is not without danger
we might make trial of it for three months, and then judge how it answers; three months are soon over.

notes.text: The voice closes the argument with a dry, deflating observation of her own, implying the risk is small and the trial will pass quickly; the writer's 'and see' invited a verdict, and this supplies it in her manner.
notes.after: three months are soon over.

lessons: Your draft states each point in a short, plain sentence, one after another; Austen carries several points in one balanced period, so the proposal, the cause, and the proof support one another and the main point lands late. Practise joining two or three of your short sentences with a semicolon or ', and', and let a dry short clause close the argument rather than begin it.

outline.gist: switch to a four-day week
people burned out; best engineer just quit
studies show productivity stays the same or goes up
it would help with hiring
it is risky and clients might not like it
try it for three months and see

plan.gist: propose four days and give the immediate cause: worn-out people, the cleverest man gone
plan.why: the urgency supports the proposal in the same period, and the main point lands late

plan.gist: proof of equal or greater work, and the advantage in engaging new people
plan.why: the proof and the benefit form one turn: the change is both reasonable and useful

plan.gist: own the danger and the clients' dislike; propose a three-month trial; close dry
plan.why: owning the risk before the trial makes the proposal moderate, and a short closing clause lands the verdict

faults.quote: It has been found, too, that as much is done in four days as in five, or more
faults.why: The writer's 'studies' are reduced to an impersonal 'it has been found'. The source of the evidence is gone, and it was the argument's support.

faults.quote: the cleverest of our number has just quitted his situation
faults.why: 'Best engineer' becomes 'cleverest', which is a different quality from being the best at the work. The engineer's role is dropped. The pronoun 'his' invents a gender.

faults.quote: three months are soon over
faults.why: This is a new assertion that the trial is short and the risk small. It adds a claim and slightly softens the writer's acknowledged risk. The note admits the addition but calls it a 'liberty', not a mending of a fault.

faults.quote: do our business in four days rather than five
faults.why: The phrase is stiff and unidiomatic. Austen would say something nearer 'confine our labours to four days in the week'. 'Do our business' reads as modern prose in period dress.

faults.quote: the people are worn out
faults.why: 'The people' is vague and faintly odd for colleagues, where Austen would say 'our people' or 'our associates'. The clause also reads as flat.

faults.quote: assist us in engaging new people
faults.why: This is a plain paraphrase with little Austenian turn or irony. The second half of the rewrite relies on semicolon chains but has few of her characteristic balanced antitheses.

faults.quote: cites Mansfield Park, ch. 43, ¶ 2
faults.why: The citations look invented or unverifiable. The notes give precise chapter and paragraph numbers with no matching passage.

faults.quote: cites Lady Susan, ch. 38, ¶ 3
faults.why: Lady Susan is an epistolary novella with letters, not chapters up to 38. The cited source cannot support 'three months are soon over'.

faults.quote: Judgement in abstract nouns: “I am of opinion that we should do our business in four days rather than five”
faults.why: The label does not match the quote. The sentence has one abstract noun, 'opinion', and no abstract-noun judgement structure. The 'Ironic verdict' label on a mild trial proposal is likewise mislabeled.

faults.quote: Clauses balanced in one period
faults.why: The quoted sentence is one simple semicolon join, not a balanced period. The claim overstates what was done.

faults.quote: proposal with cause (propose four days and give the immediate cause: worn-out people, the cleverest man gone; why: the urgency supports the proposal in the same period, and the main point lands late)
faults.why: The outline says the main point lands late, but the rewrite opens with the proposal and keeps the writer's order. The outline and lesson misdescribe the rewrite, which weakens the teaching.

faults.quote: let a dry short clause close the argument rather than begin it
faults.why: The advice is sound, but the writer's draft already closed on 'see'. The lesson implies a change in the writer's habit that the rewrite and notes do not show.

judge.verdict: A readable, mostly faithful Austenish rewrite that keeps the argument's order, but it loses 'studies' and 'best engineer', adds a closing claim, and is only moderately idiomatic. The notes are the weakest part: the citations look fabricated, several labels do not fit their quotes, and the outline misdescribes the structure.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all sorry for it; I was, in truth, relieved. I had been in dread of the dinner the whole week, and I was not proud of it.

I told her that it was very well, and that we should do it another time; but I did not think we should.

rows.text: When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all sorry for it; I was, in truth, relieved. I had been in dread of the dinner the whole week, and I was not proud of it.

notes.after: When Dana put off our dinner, I was not at all sorry for it; I was, in truth, relieved.
I was not at all sorry for it

rows.text: I told her that it was very well, and that we should do it another time; but I did not think we should.

notes.after: I told her that it was very well, and that we should do it another time
but I did not think we should

lessons: Your passage speaks in short, plain sentences; Austen builds one period out of two or three of them and lets the verdict arrive by understatement. Practise joining the event to the feeling with a semicolon, and putting the reply into reported speech so the final doubt can fall quietly at the end.

outline.gist: Dana cancels the dinner
narrator is not upset; is relieved
had dreaded it all week; not proud of that
tells Dana it is fine, and they will do it another time
does not think they will

plan.gist: the cancellation and the relief in one period
plan.why: the reversal—not sorry, but relieved—is the point, and it should land at once

plan.gist: the week's dread and the narrator's not being proud of it
plan.why: the relief needs its reason, and the self-verdict tempers it

plan.gist: what was said and what was thought, the doubt last
plan.why: the outward civility and the inward reservation belong together; the doubt is the verdict

faults.quote: I was not at all sorry for it; I was, in truth, relieved.
faults.why: The sentence is the original reworded lightly, with only a semicolon and 'in truth' added. Austen would build a fuller periodic sentence with subordinate clauses and wry commentary. This is modern prose in period costume.

faults.quote: I had been in dread of the dinner the whole week, and I was not proud of it.
faults.why: It stays flat and paratactic. It has none of Austen's gradation, irony or generalizing frame, and 'I was not proud of it' reads as a paraphrase. First-person confession is not Austen's usual register either.

faults.quote: I was not at all sorry for it
faults.why: The original says 'wasn't upset at all'. 'Not sorry' shifts the sense slightly from not distressed to not regretful. It is small, but it is a change of word.

faults.quote: I was not proud of it.
faults.why: 'It' is ambiguous. It could refer to the dinner or the dread rather than the relief, and the original's 'I'm not proud of that' is looser. The self-judgement is blurred.

faults.quote: I told her that it was very well, and that we should do it another time; but I did not think we should.
faults.why: 'it was very well' is odd for 'it was fine', and 'do it another time' is modern and colloquial. The closing 'we should' is clipped and stiff, and loses the original's present-tense 'I don't think we will'.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 50, ¶ 9
faults.why: Paragraph-level citations like these look invented and unverifiable. They are not shown to illustrate the named move, and the notes cite sources for a move the rewrite barely performs.

faults.quote: Ironic verdict: “but I did not think we should” — cites Emma, ch. 21, ¶ 53
faults.why: The move is described as irony, but the sentence is a plain restatement of the original, so the note overstates the change. 'Speech reported' is also barely a change, since the original was already reported.

faults.quote: Practise joining the event to the feeling with a semicolon, and putting the reply into reported speech
faults.why: The advice is thin and mechanical. It names punctuation, not Austen's real moves such as irony, a generalizing frame, or free indirect style. The original reply was already reported, so the lesson is partly inaccurate.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: event and true feeling
faults.why: The 'as the voice would build it' outline is almost identical to the writer's order, and the rewrite changes nothing structurally. It adds no real structural insight, although the order was already sound.

judge.verdict: The meaning and feeling are kept, but the rewrite is a thin, nearly literal reshuffle with a few archaisms, so it reads little like Austen. The notes cite dubious sources and the lesson is shallow.
judge.sense_note: No fault of sense in the draft; none introduced.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent a message unto me, saying, We must needs talk together. And I knew straightway what that meant.

And on the morrow we met together at an house of drink in the midst of the city: and he was there already, and he looked upon his phone, and his countenance was troubled. And he said unto me, I am not ready for a grave matter: it is not thou, but I.

And I would have wept, but I wept not: I bowed my head, and said, It is well. And I walked home in the rain, and did eat a whole measure of ice cream.

And my friend with whom I dwelt thought that my grief was more than was meet. Peradventure I was; but it was still a grief unto me.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: and he was there already, and he looked upon his phone, and his countenance was troubled
And he said unto me, I am not ready for a grave matter: it is not thou, but I.
it is not thou, but I

notes.after: but it was still a grief unto me

lessons: The chief difference is the sentence: the writer's page runs in short separate units of five to fifteen words, while the King James Bible lays clause beside clause with "and" and lets most narrative sentences stretch past twenty words. Practise joining the small events of a scene into balanced clauses, and reserving the short sentence for the turn or the verdict.

outline.gist: Ryan's midnight message: we need to talk
the narrator knows at once what it means
the meeting at the coffee shop downtown; he is there, on his phone, nervous
he is not ready for something serious; it is not her, it is him
she wants to cry but does not; nods and says okay; walks home in the rain; eats ice cream
the roommate thinks she overreacted; maybe she did; it still hurt

plan.gist: And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent a message, saying they must needs talk together
plan.why: the voice opens a new turn of the story with the time, and joins the message and its content in one clause

plan.gist: and I knew straightway what that meant
plan.why: a short verdict, kept short so the knowing lands hard

plan.gist: on the morrow they met at a house of drink in the midst of the city; he was there already, looking upon his phone, troubled in countenance
plan.why: the place is set before the scene, then his signs given gravely

plan.gist: he said unto her, I am not ready for a grave matter: it is not thou, but I
plan.why: the parting speech is given in full, in direct speech, so the blow falls as spoken

plan.gist: she would have wept but wept not; she bowed her head and said it is well; she walked home in the rain and ate a whole measure of ice cream
plan.why: the feeling is given by its sign, and the three acts laid side by side with and

plan.gist: her friend thought her grief more than was meet; peradventure it was, but it was still a grief unto her
plan.why: the judgment and the admission close the matter, the last clause given its own weight

faults.quote: my friend with whom I dwelt
faults.why: The writer's 'roommate' becomes a 'friend'. This adds a relationship the draft did not state, and it reshapes the dismissive note of the roommate's remark.

faults.quote: I bowed my head, and said, It is well.
faults.why: 'Nodded and said okay' is flat, deflated acceptance. 'It is well' is a scriptural phrase of serene resignation (2 Kings 4:26), so it shifts the feeling toward peace. 'Bowed my head' also changes a nod, an act of assent, into one of submission.

faults.quote: and he looked upon his phone
faults.why: The writer's 'scrolling' is lost. The detail that he was absorbed in his phone, rather than merely looking at it, is dulled.

faults.quote: and his countenance was troubled
faults.why: The draft says he 'looked nervous'. 'Troubled' is a nearby word but not the same feeling, and it loses the sense of anxiety about what he was about to say.

faults.quote: an house of drink
faults.why: The KJV has 'an house', but 'house of drink' is not a phrase it uses. It reads as an invented, slightly comic circumlocution for 'coffee shop'.

faults.quote: a grave matter
faults.why: This is stiff and abstract, and it does not match the KJV's concrete diction. It also changes 'something serious' into a solemn phrase that sounds odd in a breakup speech.

faults.quote: did eat a whole measure of ice cream
faults.why: 'Measure' for 'pint' is a vague substitution, and the mock-biblical phrasing tips into unintended comedy. The ice cream sits awkwardly in an otherwise solemn register.

faults.quote: it is not thou, but I
faults.why: The phrase is grammatical but abrupt. It reads as a stilted rendering of the cliché 'it's not you, it's me' and loses the writer's two-beat rhythm.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “it is not thou, but I” — cites Acts 10:19
faults.why: The note promises '-eth and -est', but the rewrite has no such forms. Only one 'thou' is shown, so the note overstates what was done.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “but it was still a grief unto me” — cites Job 30:26
faults.why: 'Thereof' and 'wherefore' do not appear in the rewrite. Several real archaisms, such as 'straightway', 'on the morrow', 'peradventure', 'meet' and 'must needs', go unnamed.

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and”: “and he was there already, and he looked upon his phone, and his countenance was troubled” — cites Acts 10:4
faults.why: The cited verse does not obviously show this and-chaining. The source choice looks loose, and the note gives little evidence that the move matches the KJV.

faults.quote: lets most narrative sentences stretch past twenty words
faults.why: The lesson urges long balanced clause-chains, but the rewrite keeps many short sentences and only partly joins events. The lesson and the example do not fully match, and the lesson makes essentially one point.

judge.verdict: A faithful, mostly well-ordered KJV pastiche with sound archaic phrasing, but a few shifts in meaning ('friend', 'It is well', 'troubled'), some awkward inventions ('house of drink', 'measure'), and notes whose labels and citations overstate or misfit what is in the text. The lesson is useful but narrow.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at the end of the week, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto us; and they had a great truck and two little children. And the father seemed a good man; but his sister was somewhat aloof.

And straightway my mother baked cakes for them, and brought them unto them: for she desired to know all things concerning them, whence they came, and what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and had no wife; for he was divorced. And the countenance of my mother was changed, and I knew what was in her heart: for she had sought these many years to give me in marriage.

rows.text: And it came to pass at the end of the week, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto us; and they had a great truck and two little children. And the father seemed a good man; but his sister was somewhat aloof.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother—'The mom is kind of standoffish'—but your third paragraph says the father is single and divorced. A wife or former wife cannot be living with him as the children's mother if he is single. I made the standoffish woman the father's sister, who came with the household, so the family hangs together: a father, his sister, and two little children.
notes.after: but his sister was somewhat aloof
And it came to pass at the end of the week, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto us
next unto us

rows.text: And straightway my mother baked cakes for them, and brought them unto them: for she desired to know all things concerning them, whence they came, and what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And straightway my mother baked cakes for them, and brought them unto them: for she desired to know all things concerning them

rows.text: And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and had no wife; for he was divorced. And the countenance of my mother was changed, and I knew what was in her heart: for she had sought these many years to give me in marriage.

notes.after: And the countenance of my mother was changed

lessons: The chief difference is that your page tells the news in short, bare sentences, while the Authorized Version lays clause beside clause with 'and' and lets each sentence carry two or three turns of the matter. Practise joining your short sentences into one grave, balanced movement, and showing feeling by its outward sign—a changed countenance—rather than naming it.

outline.gist: a new family moves in next door, with a huge truck and two little children
the father seems nice, the woman standoffish
my mother bakes cookies at once and wants to learn where they came from, their work, their church
the father is a lawyer, single, divorced
my mother's look; I know she is thinking of setting me up

plan.gist: And it came to pass at the end of the week, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto us; and they had a great truck and two little children
plan.why: the voice opens a new turn with 'And it came to pass' and sets the place and the household before the persons.

plan.gist: And the father seemed a good man; but his sister was somewhat aloof
plan.why: the voice gives the two persons in one balanced sentence, the pleasant before the reserved.

plan.gist: And straightway my mother baked cakes for them, and brought them unto them: for she desired to know all things concerning them, whence they came, and what they did for work, and whether they went to church
plan.why: the outward deed comes first, then the mother's motive after 'for,' as the Bible gives the act and then the heart.

plan.gist: And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and had no wife; for he was divorced
plan.why: the news is set as a turn with 'And it came to pass,' the fact before the correction.

plan.gist: And the countenance of my mother was changed, and I knew what was in her heart: for she had sought these many years to give me in marriage
plan.why: the feeling is shown by its outward sign, the changed countenance, and the mother's long purpose closes the matter where it lands.

faults.quote: And it came to pass at the end of the week
faults.why: The writer said 'last weekend'. 'At the end of the week' is vaguer and changes the timing slightly. 'The first day of the week' or 'the sabbath' was not used either.

faults.quote: his sister was somewhat aloof
faults.why: The mending invents a new person (the sister). The writer's 'mom' is the children's mother, and 'standoffish' becomes the milder 'somewhat aloof'. The 'kind of' hedge is kept, but the invented relation is a heavy choice where a looser 'the woman' would have sufficed. It is reported, but the added sister is a fabricated fact.

faults.quote: baked cakes for them, and brought them unto them
faults.why: 'Cookies' becomes 'cakes', which is acceptable, but 'brought them unto them' is an addition (the writer never said she delivered them) and is clumsy repetition.

faults.quote: And it came to pass that the father was a lawyer, and had no wife; for he was divorced.
faults.why: The writer's 'It turns out' (a discovery) is rendered as an event happening, 'it came to pass that the father was a lawyer', which is a misuse of the formula. 'Single. Well, divorced' is a self-correction; 'for he was divorced' turns it into a causal explanation.

faults.quote: for she had sought these many years to give me in marriage
faults.why: 'She has been trying to set me up for years' is present perfect, ongoing. The rewrite makes it past and complete, and 'many years' is slightly inflated. The mother's look is turned into a 'countenance changed' with no hint of her thought, though the narrator's inference is kept.

faults.quote: what they did for work
faults.why: Modern phrase, not KJV idiom; the voice would say 'what manner of work they did' or 'what was their occupation/labour'. 'Great truck' and 'lawyer' are also anachronistic words that go unadapted (a lawyer appears in the KJV, but 'truck' does not).

faults.quote: next unto us
faults.why: 'Unto' is used where 'next to' or 'next door' would be idiomatic; the cited Ruth 1:18 does not support 'next unto'. The real KJV would say 'dwelt in the house next to ours' or 'hard by'.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 39:13
faults.why: The citation for 'And it came to pass' is loosely apt, but the phrase appears in hundreds of places and this verse is arbitrary. The 'unto' note citing Ruth 1:18 is also questionable, and the notes label 'thereof, wherefore' which are not in the rewrite.

faults.quote: showing feeling by its outward sign—a changed countenance—rather than naming it
faults.why: The lesson is sound but the notes explain few moves and miss the 'And' parataxis across sentences, the doubled 'it came to pass' (used twice, where the repetition reads as a tic), and the missing paragraph on the mother's curiosity.

faults.quote: But his sister was somewhat aloof
faults.why: The mend resolves the contradiction but it creates a new fact and leaves the children's mother unexplained. It is reported honestly, but the fix is more invasive than needed.

judge.verdict: A competent KJV pastiche with the right parataxis and a reported mending, but the invented sister adds a fact, 'it came to pass' is misused for a discovery and overused, and a few modern words and tense shifts weaken fidelity and voice.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Unto the crew, greeting.

And behold, this is the word I send unto you: the launch is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday. And the lawyers have not yet set their hand to the leaf of the price; and I would not that we should send it forth without it.

And I pray you, have ye your parts of the deck made ready by Wednesday at noon. And if any of you be hindered, tell me this day, and not the morrow.

I thank you. The salutation of Sam with mine own hand.

notes.after: And behold, this is the word I send unto you: the launch is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday.
the leaf of the price

lessons: The chief difference is that your note moves in short modern bursts, while the Author's manner is to lay clause beside clause with and, and to open with And or Behold. Practise joining the news to its reason in one long sentence, and turning requests into the imperative with ye and the old verbs.

outline.gist: Hi team
the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed the pricing page; do not ship without it
have your deck sections done by Wednesday noon
tell me today if blocked, not tomorrow

plan.gist: Unto the crew, greeting
plan.why: The epistle names the addressees first, as the writer's salutation does.

plan.gist: the launch is moved from Tuesday unto Thursday
plan.why: The tidings come before the hindrance, as the writer gave them, so the reader hears the change first.

plan.gist: the lawyers have not set their hand to the leaf of the price; do not send it forth without it
plan.why: The hindrance follows the news and explains the caution, keeping the writer's order.

plan.gist: have ye your parts of the deck made ready by Wednesday at noon
plan.why: The charge to the crew comes next, with its set time, as the writer ordered it.

plan.gist: if any be hindered, tell me this day, and not the morrow
plan.why: The second charge stands last among the commands, as the writer's turn of urgency.

plan.gist: I thank you; the salutation of Sam with mine own hand
plan.why: The epistle ends with thanks and the writer's own hand, where the draft signs only the name.

faults.quote: The salutation of Sam with mine own hand.
faults.why: The email is not handwritten, so this adds a claim the writer did not make. It is a borrowing from 1 Cor 16:21 and reads as a flourish rather than a rendering of 'Thanks, Sam'.

faults.quote: the lawyers have not yet set their hand to the leaf of the price
faults.why: 'Legal' is a department and 'pricing page' is a web page. 'Lawyers' and 'leaf of the price' shift the sense slightly and blur what is being approved.

faults.quote: Unto the crew, greeting.
faults.why: 'Quick update' is dropped. 'Crew' is a modern, nautical word, not 'team', and sits oddly in KJV diction.

faults.quote: have ye your parts of the deck made ready by Wednesday at noon
faults.why: 'Have ye ... made ready' is not KJV syntax. The Bible would say 'let your parts ... be made ready' or 'make ye ready'. It is archaic-sounding but built like modern English.

faults.quote: I thank you.
faults.why: This is flat and modern in cadence. The KJV pattern would be 'I give you thanks' or 'grace be with you'. The ending is mostly a single borrowed epistolary line.

faults.quote: I would not that we should send it forth without it.
faults.why: The rhythm is stilted, and 'without it' repeats against 'it' as the object. The phrase is only half-idiomatic KJV.

faults.quote: Thou and thee, -eth and -est: “And I pray you, have ye your parts of the deck made ready by Wednesday at noon.” — cites Psalms 6:5
faults.why: The quoted sentence has no thou, thee, -eth or -est, only 'ye' and 'pray you'. The move is mislabeled and the citation is a poor fit.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “Unto the crew, greeting.” — cites Matthew 14:16
faults.why: The sentence contains only 'unto'. 'Thereof' and 'wherefore' do not appear, so the note names words that were not used.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of”: “the leaf of the price” — cites 1 Corinthians 14:16
faults.why: The citation is weak, and 'leaf of the price' is an awkward coinage rather than a genuine KJV genitive.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 4:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The closing is a direct borrowing from the Pauline epistles (1 Cor 16:21), and the only substantive addition. It goes unnamed and unsourced, as do the 'this day... the morrow' phrasing and 'I pray you'.

faults.quote: Practise joining the news to its reason in one long sentence, and turning requests into the imperative with ye and the old verbs.
faults.why: The rewrite does not join news and reason in one long sentence, so the lesson does not match the text. It is generic, and it gives no reason why the technique works or how to carry it into the writer's own prose.

faults.quote: The tidings come before the hindrance, as the writer gave them
faults.why: The structure notes mostly say the order was kept and offer little transferable insight. Several 'why' lines only restate the writer's order.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps all the facts and the email's order and adds only a small false flourish ('with mine own hand'). The KJV flavor is shallow, and some syntax and word choices ('crew', 'have ye ... made ready') are off. The notes mislabel moves and cite sources that do not fit, and the lesson is generic and does not match what the rewrite actually did.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Let our town shut up Main Street against cars at the end of the week. For the leaving of cars in the midst of the town is a sore trouble, and the paths are too narrow for carriages: and other towns have done this thing, and their booths prosper more than they did before.

And some that keep the booths will say unto us, The guests cannot come unto us: but they shall be wont to it; for verily the most part of the people walk from the garage already.

And let us try it this summer, and prove it.

faults.quote: And there be works which shew that the labour abideth the same
faults.why: The writer said 'studies show productivity stays the same or goes up'. 'Works which shew' is vague; 'studies' is lost, so the evidence turns into 'works' that could mean deeds.

faults.quote: the best of our workmen hath even now left us

faults.quote: they that hire us may not be pleased

faults.quote: And we might prove it for the space of three months, and see.

faults.quote: I think it meet that we should turn unto a week of four days

faults.quote: the labour abideth the same, or waxeth greater

faults.quote: help us in the taking of new men

faults.quote: I know there is danger in it

faults.quote:

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences with "and" and "for," and naming a modern thing by its work in the sentence rather than by its modern title.

faults.quote: the voice opens with the main thing as a plain declaration, not as a business suggestion

faults.quote: I was eased

faults.quote: And it came to pass, when Dana put off our dinner
faults.why: The modern name 'Dana' and 'put off our dinner' sit uneasily with the archaic diction. KJV would say 'feast' or 'supper'. 'Put off' is not KJV usage for cancelling.

faults.why: 'Not grieved at all' is a modern intensifier, and 'verily' used to introduce a contrast with 'eased' reads as a pastiche. The sentence is stiff.

faults.quote: cites 1 Thessalonians 3:4
faults.why: The cited verses do not exemplify the moves they are attached to. 1 Thess 3:4 is not an 'it came to pass' opening, Mark 9:12 and John 14:29 are weak matches, and Matthew 18:31 is not a notable 'thereof' example. The citations look arbitrary.

faults.quote: the voice makes the unspoken contrast plain between what the narrator said aloud and what the narrator truly thought
faults.why: The rewrite adds nothing to make this contrast plain beyond what the draft already had, so the notes claim a liberty that was not really taken. The 'but I do not think we shall' is the writer's own line.

faults.quote: Practise opening turns with that formula and bringing speech in with said unto
faults.why: The lesson is a generic checklist of archaisms. It gives little on why the paired clauses suit the content or how the writer could reuse the structural moves in their own voice. The advice to 'let each paragraph close on the thought the writer kept back' is the writer's own structure.

faults.quote: It is well; and we shall do it another time: but I do not think we shall.
faults.why: Colon and semicolon stacking is not KJV punctuation habit in this way, and 'but I do not think we shall' is the modern phrase left almost unchanged. The ending is therefore flat and not rendered in the voice.

judge.verdict: Meaning and feeling are preserved and the structure kept, but the voice is mostly thin archaisms ('verily', 'thereof') over modern phrasing, with a tense slip. The notes cite apparently arbitrary verses and the lesson is generic.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Last weekend, a new family moved in next door, with a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seemed nice. The woman I took for their mother wasn't cold, exactly — she just kept to herself.

Right away, my mother made them a plate of something sweet. She wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for a living, whether they went to church.

As it turned out, the dad was a lawyer, and he was single. Well — it didn't work out. The woman I'd taken for their mother was his sister. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She'd been trying to set me up for years. That's what mothers do — they keep at it.

faults.quote: Well — it didn't work out.

faults.quote: That's what mothers do — they keep at it.
faults.why: This adds a new general claim and a warmer attitude toward the mother. The notes disclose it as a liberty, but it still shifts the writer's wry, slightly weary tone.

faults.quote: Last weekend, a new family moved in next door, with a huge truck and two little kids.
faults.why: The Obama flavour is thin. Apart from the final aphorism and a few dashes, it is a mild tidy-up of the draft, without his rhythm, his self-deprecating humour or his build-up to a larger point.

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: This is confusing and inaccurate. The rewrite's paragraph 1 renders the writer's paragraph 1 whole, and the later paragraph merely borrows from it.

faults.quote: Building in threes: “where they came from, what they did for a living, whether they went to church”
faults.why: The writer already had the three questions. Crediting this as an Obama move overstates the change, and the cited firefighters memorial is an odd source.

faults.quote: Not this, but that: “The woman I took for their mother wasn't cold, exactly — she just kept to herself.”

faults.quote: Practise joining short sentences with ", and" or an em-dash
faults.why: The advice is fairly generic and does not match what the rewrite actually changed. The rewrite leaves many sentences short, and the notes do not explain why the closing general truth works.

judge.verdict: It catches and reports the real contradiction with a coherent fix (the sister), and it keeps the structure. But it loses the cookies and the word 'divorced', places the reveal awkwardly, and sounds only lightly like Obama. The notes are thin and loosely cited.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

rewrite:
Here's the thing: we should close Main Street to cars on the weekends. Trying to park downtown is a nightmare, and the walks are too narrow for a family with small children. Other towns have done this, and their shops aren't just getting by—they're doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that their customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. The truth is, most folks walk in from where they parked anyway.

That's why we should try it this summer.

plan.why: Open with the shared “we” and the thing to be done, then the felt reason, so listeners recognize their own town.

plan.why: Prove it works before meeting the doubt, so the doubt answers itself.

faults.quote: the walks are too narrow for a family with small children
faults.why: The writer said 'sidewalks are too narrow for strollers'. 'Walks' is an odd shortening of 'sidewalks', and 'a family with small children' changes the concrete detail (strollers) into a vaguer, slightly different image.

faults.quote: the walks are too narrow
faults.why: 'Walks' for sidewalks is unidiomatic for Obama and slightly confusing next to 'walk in' in the next paragraph.

faults.quote: their shops aren't just getting by—they're doing better than ever
faults.why: This adds 'getting by', a claim that the shops had been struggling, which the writer did not state. The 'not just X but Y' inflates the claim.

faults.quote: most folks walk in from where they parked anyway
faults.why: The writer said 'walk from the garage'. 'Where they parked' loses the specific garage and weakens the writer's concrete point.

faults.quote: But they'll get used to it.
faults.why: The writer's weak, dismissive answer to the objection is kept untouched and not flagged. The rewrite does not note the weakness, and the notes do not discuss how to give the objection a better answer.

faults.quote: Here's the thing: we should close Main Street
faults.why: The rewrite is mostly the writer's sentences with a few verbal tics ('Here's the thing', 'folks', 'The truth is', 'That's why'). It lacks Obama's balanced clauses, rhythm, concession and the 'I know some will say...' device. It reads as modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: But they'll get used to it.
faults.why: Obama would concede fairly and answer with reasoning, not a curt dismissal. The 'fair hearing' of the other side is claimed in the structure notes but not done in the text.

faults.quote: cites Weekly Address, 20 December 2014, ¶ 8
faults.why: The note calls 'a family with small children' 'One American's story', but there is no individual story, only a generic family. The move label is inaccurate. The paragraph-level citations are also unverifiable and probably decorative.

faults.quote: The voice turns to the listener before the proposal, as he does at a podium
faults.why: 'Here's the thing' does not turn to the listener, and the note describes 'the shared we' as being in the sentence, though 'we' was already in the original ('Our town'). It overstates what changed.

faults.quote: The antithesis framing makes the evidence land
faults.why: The note presents the added 'getting by' implication as a virtue, but it adds an unsupported claim. Reporting it as a 'liberty' does not mend that.

faults.quote: proposal and problem (Close Main Street to cars on weekends; parking is a nightmare...
faults.why: The outline claims the voice would build the piece differently, but the rewrite keeps the writer's order unchanged. The 'as the voice would build it' section is essentially the same as the draft, so it does not actually show a different structure.

faults.quote: Practise joining a claim to its reason in one sentence
faults.why: The lesson says the rewrite joins claims to reasons in one sentence and uses 'balanced' sentences and fair answers to the other side, but the rewrite does none of these. The advice is generic and not grounded in the text. There is also a stray escape in '\u201cwe\u201d'.

judge.verdict: A light, faithful touch-up that sprinkles Obama tics ('Here's the thing', 'folks', 'That's why') over the writer's sentences without real restructuring. It adds a 'getting by' implication and shifts concrete details, and the notes and lesson claim moves the text does not make.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

When Dana called off our dinner, I was not upset at all. The truth is, I was relieved. I had been hoping all week that something would come up, and I am not proud of that.

I told her it was fine, and that we would do it another time. But I don't think we will.

notes.text: The voice makes the quiet turn explicit — what she was told, and what is true — so the last line lands on the private truth rather than trailing off.

lessons: The chief difference is that your five sentences stay in the key of a note to yourself, while his manner says each feeling plainly and turns the paragraph on the contrast between what was said and what was true. Practise replacing the abstract word ('dreading') with the plain act that shows it, and landing the last line on the private truth.

plan.why: He turns from the feeling to what it means about the narrator, judging the relief fairly instead of hiding it.

plan.gist: The outward promise to Dana, then the quiet contradiction.
plan.why: The paragraph lands on the private truth, not on the politeness; the 'but' makes the turn audible.

faults.quote: I had been hoping all week that something would come up
faults.why: The writer said 'dreading it all week'. The rewrite swaps dread for hoping that something would come up. This is a different feeling and implies a wish for a cancellation, so it is a added detail beyond the original.

faults.quote: When Dana called off our dinner, I was not upset at all. The truth is, I was relieved.
faults.why: This is almost the writer's own prose with contractions expanded. Obama's cadence is missing: no rhythmic triplets, no 'Now,' or 'And yet', no reflective widening. It reads as modern prose with a light costume.

faults.quote: I told her it was fine, and that we would do it another time. But I don't think we will.
faults.why: It switches from 'we would' to the contraction 'don't', which is inconsistent. It also barely changes the writer's words, so the voice is thin.

faults.why: The 'not this, but that' move is claimed, but the rewrite has no such construction, only a plain 'but'. The citation is a grand eulogy that does not suit this sentence, so the source is not apt.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: The voice makes the quiet turn explicit
faults.why: The writer's original already had the turn ('I don't think we will'), and the rewrite changed almost nothing. The note overstates a change. The 'The shared we' note likewise names a move that was already in the draft ('we'd do it another time'). The 'plain talk' note claims a move that is just the writer's own 'Honestly'.

faults.quote: Practise replacing the abstract word ('dreading') with the plain act that shows it
faults.why: The lesson advises replacing 'dreading' with a plain act, but the rewrite does not do it (it swaps in 'hoping something would come up'). The lesson and the outline describe a rewrite that is not on the page, so the writer gains little.

faults.quote: I was not upset at all
faults.why: The uncontracted 'not' alongside the contracted 'don't' later in the piece makes the register uneven. 'Called off our dinner' is fine, but the whole feels stiff rather than Obama's conversational ease.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is barely changed from the draft, and it shifts 'dreading' to 'hoping something would come up', which alters the feeling. The notes cite grand speeches for moves that are absent or already in the original, and the lesson describes changes that were not made.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight, and said he needed to talk; and I knew, right off, what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee-house down town, and he was there before me, fooling with his telephone; and he looked nervous. He allowed he wasn't ready for anything serious, and then he said it wasn't me, it was him—which is a thing a body has heard before, I judge.

I wanted to cry, but I didn't. I just nodded and said it was all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate allowed I was making too much of it, and maybe I was, I reckon. But it hurt, all the same.

notes.text: The voice renders the modern scrolling as idle fiddling, which is how a Twain narrator would see a man puttering at a telephone while he waits, and it frames the nervousness without saying 'nervous' again.
notes.after: fooling with his telephone

notes.text: The voice punctures the cliché 'it isn't me, it's him' flatly, and the aside lets the narrator step out and confide, which is Twain's way of siding with the reader.

and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream
