notes.after: maybe I was, I reckon

notes.text: The voice turns the bare 'maybe' into a spoken aside, the narrator hedging and confiding at once.
notes.after: I reckon

lessons: Your draft tells it in short, plain sentences that move one step at a time; Twain tells it in long runs of clauses joined with 'and' that pile up and then turn. The chief difference is rhythm: he lets one sentence carry three or four facts before the punch, and saves a short sentence for the thing that must land hardest. Practise joining your short sentences into one long breath, and keep the last line short.

outline.gist: Ryan's midnight message and what it meant
the meeting at the coffee shop and the talk
wanting to cry, saying all right, the walk and the ice cream
the roommate's judgment, the maybe, and the lingering hurt

plan.gist: the midnight word and the knowing, in one long sentence
plan.why: The voice gives the news and its meaning in one breath, before all else, because the whole matter is in it.

plan.gist: the coffee-house meeting, his look, then what he said
plan.why: The voice sets the scene before the talk, then lets his two statements land in order, the cliché punctured with a deadpan aside.

plan.gist: the wanting to cry, the nod, the walk and the ice cream
plan.why: The voice runs the reaction into one long sentence and ends on the pint of ice cream, flat and unexplained, as the punch.

plan.gist: the roommate's judgment, the maybe, and the hurt
plan.why: The voice keeps the verdict and the doubt together, then ends on a short sentence, because a short last sentence lands hardest.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight
faults.why: The writer's 'texted' is a specific medium. 'Sent me word' blurs it and could mean a messenger or a letter, while 'telephone' later in the passage suggests a modern setting.

faults.quote: and maybe I was, I reckon
faults.why: 'Maybe' and 'I reckon' hedge twice in one clause. Twain's hedges are sharper and more deliberate, so this reads as dialect sprinkled on top.

faults.quote: He allowed he wasn't ready ... My roommate allowed I was making too much of it
faults.why: 'Allowed' is used twice as the dialect verb of speech in a short passage, which sounds mechanical and uses up the flavor.

faults.quote: fooling with his telephone
faults.why: The Huck-style dialect ('allowed', 'reckon', 'a body') is laid over a modern city scene and a modern speaker. The result is costume dialect rather than Twain's own wry narration. The piece also keeps most of the writer's short sentences ('I wanted to cry, but I didn't.'), so it shows little of the long cumulative runs Twain is known for.

faults.quote: it frames the nervousness without saying 'nervous' again
faults.why: The rewrite does say 'he looked nervous', so the note describes a change that was not made.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 13, ¶ 16
faults.why: The paragraph-level citations (ch. 13 ¶16, ch. 18 ¶83, ch. 19 ¶8, ch. 31 ¶50) are suspiciously precise and not plausibly tied to these phrases. 'Sent me word' is not a distinctive move and does not need a source.

faults.quote: Deadpan: “and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream”
faults.why: This repeats the same sentence already cited as 'cumulative'. The writer already had it deadpan, so no new move was made. Several items marked 'liberty' (the cliché aside, the 'maybe' aside) are really voice moves, which muddles the notes' categories.

faults.quote: Practise joining your short sentences into one long breath, and keep the last line short.
faults.why: The advice is sound but generic. The rewrite barely demonstrates it, since paragraph 3 is nearly unchanged and the sentences are only lightly joined by semicolons. The writer gets little concrete model of how Twain's pile-up and turn works.

judge.verdict: A faithful, readable rewrite with a few good Twain touches ('a thing a body has heard before, I judge'). Its dialect is somewhat superficial, and the notes carry inaccurate claims and dubious citations. The teaching is thin because the long-sentence lesson is barely demonstrated.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

I made her his sister—the smallest change that lets her be standoffish, live with them, and not be his wife. Everything else said of her stays.

plan.gist: A new family moved in next door last Saturday, with a huge truck and two little young ones.
plan.why: The voice sets the scene first, plain, before any judgment; joining the arrival and the household into one sentence keeps the breath moving.

plan.gist: Their father seems nice, but his sister is kind of offish, I judge.
plan.why: The two judgments go together in one balanced sentence, the favorable against the unfavorable, so each shows the other; 'I judge' keeps the teller in it.

plan.gist: My mother baked them cakes right off, and wanted to find out everything about them—where they came from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.
plan.why: The voice runs the welcome and the questions into one long breath, because the mother did it all in one breath; the list lands as a pile.

plan.gist: It turns out their father is a lawyer, and single—well, divorced.
plan.why: The news comes flat, and the correction 'well, divorced' is the turn, so it gets the dash and the short clause.

plan.gist: My mother got a look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking; she has been trying to make a match for me for years.
plan.why: The voice saves the joke for the end of the sentence and never explains it; the semicolon lets the last clause land as the punch line.

faults.quote: his sister is kind of offish
faults.why: The sister is an invented relation. The writer said 'the mom'. The mending is reported, but it replaces a stated fact with a guess, and 'mom' is gone entirely.

faults.quote: two little young ones
faults.why: 'Little young ones' is redundant and clumsy. It also changes 'kids'.

faults.quote: cakes
faults.why: The writer wrote 'cookies'. Swapping to 'cakes' changes a fact for period flavor.

faults.quote: right off, and wanted to find out
faults.why: The writer's sentence 'She wanted to find out everything about them' has been fused with the baking. This is minor, but the mother's motive is now less pointed.

faults.quote: last Saturday
faults.why: The writer wrote 'last weekend'. Naming a day is an invented detail.

faults.quote: I judge.
faults.why: 'I judge' is thin, borrowed Huck dialect. The rewrite lacks Twain's comic exaggeration, simile, or irony and reads as light period dressing. Huck's narration also doesn't use 'make a match'.

faults.quote: I knew exactly what she was thinking; she has been trying to make a match for me for years.
faults.why: The modern 'exactly' and the present-perfect 'has been trying' with a semicolon sit oddly in a Huck-like register. The punchline is plain, with no Twain-like inflation.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 15, ¶ 42
faults.why: The citations are specific, but chapter and paragraph numbers are implausible and the passages are not clearly apt. Notes label 'deadpan' and 'cumulative sentence' for fairly ordinary sentences, and don't report changes such as 'cakes', 'Saturday', or 'young ones'.

faults.quote: The narrator breaks off to confide his own judgment, as Huck does with 'I reckon'
faults.why: The rewrite uses 'I judge', not 'I reckon', and the narrator's sex is assumed.

faults.quote: his sister is kind of offish
faults.why: The mending is reasonable, but a sister is not the only fix and it stays a guess. It also makes the family odd, since a divorced father with a sister and two kids is unexplained.

faults.quote: Twain tells it aloud in one long breath
faults.why: The lesson is partly vague. The rewrite's sentences are not notably longer than the draft's, so the claim isn't borne out in the text.

judge.verdict: Competent and clear, and it catches the contradiction and reports it. The Twain voice is faint, though, and there are small unreported invented details (cakes, Saturday, young ones). The notes cite shaky sources and over-claim the long-breath lesson.

plan.why: The reason rides after the news in one long run, deadpan, so the obstacle lands without being argued.

plan.gist: pages done by Wednesday noon, and the noon is meant
plan.why: The command is polite and plain, and the aside keeps the deadline from being softened.

plan.gist: if held up, he wants to hear of it today, not tomorrow
plan.why: The second request turns on the flat opposition of today and tomorrow, the point landing at the end.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam.
plan.why: A short close, as the writer gave it.

faults.quote: and I do mean noon
faults.why: Adds an emphasis the writer never made. The original is a plain deadline with no insistence. The note admits it as a liberty, but it still changes the tone.

faults.quote: your pages done
faults.why: 'Sections of the deck' becomes 'pages'. This loses the sense of parts of a shared deck and could be read as something else.

faults.quote: the sending-out is moved
faults.why: 'Launch' becomes 'sending-out'. This is a clumsy circumlocution that blurs a product launch into something like mailing.

faults.quote: the lawyers have not yet put their names to the price-page
faults.why: 'Legal' becomes 'the lawyers' and the pricing page becomes 'price-page'. This is acceptable as period flavor but is a mild shift, and 'put their names to' is not the same as signing off.

faults.quote: I will thank you to have your pages done
faults.why: This is a stiff, huffy Victorian idiom, not Twain's vernacular humor. It reads as a schoolmaster's scolding and gives no comic observation, exaggeration or irony.

faults.quote: A quick word—the sending-out is moved from Tuesday to Thursday; the lawyers
faults.why: The semicolon and dash are only a light period costume. There is no Twainian wit, concrete simile, mock-solemnity or understatement. It is mostly the original with archaic words swapped in.

faults.quote: Friends,
faults.why: This is a plausible but weak greeting. It adds nothing Twain-like and shifts the register from 'team'.

faults.quote: I want to hear of it today, and not tomorrow.
faults.why: The sentence is slightly stilted and loses the punch of 'today, not tomorrow'. The added 'and' weakens the clipped contrast.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam.
faults.why: Merging 'Thanks,' and 'Sam' into one line loses the sign-off form of the letter.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 33, ¶ 53
faults.why: These citations are very specific and look fabricated or inapt. Huck Finn is not about price pages, and the cited paragraphs are unlikely to show the claimed moves.

faults.quote: Deadpan: “If any one of you is held up, I want to hear of it today, and not tomorrow.”
faults.why: The sentence has no deadpan quality. The label is generous. The 'narrator's aside' label is also wrong, because the dash phrase is an imperative emphasis, not an aside.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence
faults.why: This repeats the vernacular-voice note on the same sentence under a different label, so the notes are padded. Paragraph 1 and paragraph 4 also have no notes, and the 'Thanks, Sam.' change goes unreported.

faults.quote: replacing the office words (update, sign off, ship, blocked, deck) with plain words that say what is actually done
faults.why: The advice is generic. The rewrite swaps in 'sending-out' and 'pages', which are vaguer, not plainer, so the lesson contradicts its own example. It gives no Twain technique such as understatement, concrete comparison or comic exaggeration.

judge.verdict: A faithful, short email, but the voice is thin: archaic phrasing with no real Twain humor, and 'sending-out' and 'pages' are muddy. The notes use dubious Huck Finn citations with mislabeled moves, and the lesson is generic and at odds with the rewrite.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
I judge we ought to close Main Street to cars on Saturdays and Sundays, and let it be a street for people on foot. There is no small trouble in finding a place to put a car downtown; and the sidewalks are too narrow for a baby-carriage to pass. They have tried it in other towns, and the shops there are doing better than ever they did before.

There will be some of the storekeepers that will raise a cry and say the customers can't get to them. But they will get used to it, for the truth is that most people walk from the livery stable anyway.

We ought to try it this summer.

rows.text: I judge we ought to close Main Street to cars on Saturdays and Sundays, and let it be a street for people on foot. There is no small trouble in finding a place to put a car downtown; and the sidewalks are too narrow for a baby-carriage to pass. They have tried it in other towns, and the shops there are doing better than ever they did before.

notes.after: I judge we ought to close Main Street to cars on Saturdays and Sundays, and let it be a street for people on foot.

notes.after: There is no small trouble in finding a place to put a car downtown; and the sidewalks are too narrow for a baby-carriage to pass.
notes.cite: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 31, ¶ 30

notes.after: They have tried it in other towns, and the shops there are doing better than ever they did before.

notes.text: the writer stated the proposal bare; the voice makes it a man's own judgment, the way Twain's first-person narrators open an argument.
notes.after: I judge we ought to close Main Street

notes.text: the writer only said to close the street; the voice says plainly what closing it is for, which the rest of the passage points to.
notes.after: and let it be a street for people on foot

lessons: Your draft states each point in a short bare sentence, like a memo. Twain's narrator argues it as a man talking: he opens with his own judgment, piles the reasons with 'and' and a semicolon, and saves the one short sentence for the final call. Practise joining your short sentences into longer cumulative runs that end on the turn.

parking downtown is a nightmare; sidewalks too narrow for strollers
other towns have done this; their shops doing better than ever
some business owners will complain customers can't get to them
they'll get used to it

plan.gist: I judge we ought to close Main Street to cars on Saturdays and Sundays
plan.why: the news goes first, in the teller's own judgment, with no throat-clearing

plan.gist: no small trouble putting a car downtown; sidewalks too narrow for a baby-carriage
plan.why: the particulars come before the proof, joined with '; and' so they pile up in one breath

plan.gist: they have tried it in other towns, and the shops there are doing better than ever they did before
plan.why: the proof is stated flat, with no exclamation, so the surprise lands by itself

plan.gist: some of the storekeepers will raise a cry that the customers can't get to them
plan.why: the one objection is named plainly, in the voice's own words for it

plan.gist: they will get used to it; the truth is most people walk from the livery stable anyway
plan.why: the two short answers are joined in one run that ends on 'anyway' as the turn

plan.gist: we ought to try it this summer
plan.why: a short sentence of its own paragraph lands the proposal

faults.quote: and let it be a street for people on foot
faults.why: Adds a purpose clause the writer did not state. The note then claims the rest of the passage points to it, which is a stretch; it is an addition.

faults.quote: Saturdays and Sundays
faults.why: The writer said 'weekends'. This is a minor narrowing, though defensible.

faults.quote: the livery stable
faults.why: The writer's 'garage' is replaced with a period anachronism. The rewrite also uses 'car' and 'Main Street' beside it, so the setting is incoherent: cars exist, yet people walk from a livery stable.

faults.quote: most people walk from the livery stable anyway
faults.why: The original's logic is that people already walk from the garage, so closing the street changes little. A livery stable holds horses, not parked cars. The logic is muddled by the swap and the mismatch with 'car' is unreported.

faults.quote: But they will get used to it, for the truth is
faults.why: The writer's weak answer ('they'll get used to it. Honestly...') is merged into one sentence with a causal 'for'. This makes 'get used to it' depend on the walking claim, subtly changing the relation. No sense note reports it.

faults.quote: There is no small trouble in finding a place to put a car downtown
faults.why: This softens the punchy 'nightmare' into a stiff litotes. It is not Twain's usual hyperbole and loses the writer's force. 'A baby-carriage' is fine, but the sentence has no Twain humor or exaggeration.

faults.quote: I judge we ought to close Main Street
faults.why: 'I judge' is a Huck-style dialect marker, but it is dropped onto a civic-argument register with no further humor. The overall rewrite is a light period-flavored paraphrase, not Twain's wit, irony or digression.

faults.quote: There will be some of the storekeepers that will raise a cry and say
faults.why: Clumsy and awkward ('some of the storekeepers that will... will'). 'Raise a cry' is stilted.

faults.quote: doing better than ever they did before
faults.why: 'Than ever they did before' is redundant and archaic-sounding rather than idiomatic Twain.

faults.quote: cites A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 26, ¶ 4
faults.why: The citations (chapter and paragraph numbers) look fabricated or unverifiable. 'The narrator's aside' mislabels a plain proposal opening. Tom Sawyer ch. 31 and Innocents Abroad ch. 27 are cited for lines that are not drawn from them.

faults.quote: [move] Deadpan: “They have tried it in other towns...
faults.why: Nothing deadpan was done; the sentence is a flat restatement. The note overclaims a move.

faults.quote: [move] Cumulative sentence: “But they will get used to it, for the truth is that most people walk from the livery stable anyway.”
faults.why: The livery-stable substitution, a significant change of meaning, is not reported as a liberty. Paragraph 3 has no note, though the sentence was altered ('We should' to 'We ought to').

faults.quote: Twain's narrator argues it as a man talking: he opens with his own judgment
faults.why: The lesson is generic and does not teach Twain's actual levers (exaggeration, understatement, concrete comic specifics). It also misdescribes the rewrite, which barely joins sentences. 'Piles the reasons with and and a semicolon' is only one semicolon.

faults.quote: a short sentence of its own paragraph lands the proposal
faults.why: The 'how it is built' claims reordering benefits but the structure is identical to the writer's. The claimed differences are overstated, though keeping the structure is fine.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the argument's order but swaps 'garage' for 'livery stable', which breaks the logic beside 'car', and adds a purpose clause. The voice is thin period-flavored paraphrase with awkward phrasing, and the notes cite dubious sources and miss the real changes.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I reckon we ought to cut the week down to four days, for the people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit. The reports show the work don't fall off—it stays the same or goes up; and it would be a help in getting new hands.

I know it is a risk, and the customers might not take to it. We could try it for three months, and see.

rows.text: I reckon we ought to cut the week down to four days, for the people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit. The reports show the work don't fall off—it stays the same or goes up; and it would be a help in getting new hands.

notes.after: I reckon we ought to cut the week down to four days
for the people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit.
the best engineer we had has up and quit
notes.cite: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, ch. 29, ¶ 34

notes.after: The reports show the work don't fall off—it stays the same or goes up
notes.cite: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 33, ¶ 1

rows.text: I know it is a risk, and the customers might not take to it. We could try it for three months, and see.

lessons: Your draft is a tight office memo; Twain would say it aloud, one plain voice reasoning its way through. The chief difference is that he piles the reasons into a spoken run instead of listing them flat, and he lets the short trial sentence land last as the turn. Practise opening with the verdict and then letting the reasons pile up behind it until the last words carry the point.

outline.gist: we should switch to a four-day week
people are burned out and the best engineer just quit
studies show productivity stays the same or goes up
it would help with hiring
it is risky and clients might not like it
try it for three months and see

plan.gist: I reckon we ought to cut the week to four days, for the people are wore out and the best engineer has quit
plan.why: the voice opens with the verdict, then piles the reasons in one run so they gather weight

plan.gist: the reports show the work don't fall off, and it would help in getting new hands
plan.why: the report answers the doubt first, and the hiring help follows straight from it

plan.gist: I know it is a risk, and the customers might not take to it
plan.why: the risk is admitted plainly, before the trial, so the trial lands as the answer to it

plan.gist: we could try it for three months and see
plan.why: end on the short plain proposal, with the turn in the last words

faults.quote: The reports show the work don't fall off—it stays the same or goes up
faults.why: The writer said 'studies'; 'reports' weakens the evidential claim. 'The work' replaces 'productivity', and 'don't fall off' adds a slight shift. The meaning is mostly kept but diluted.

faults.quote: I reckon we ought to cut the week down to four days
faults.why: The writer's 'switch to a four-day week' is a change of schedule. 'Cut the week down' implies shortening work, which suggests a pay or hours reduction and subtly alters the proposal.

faults.quote: for the people are wore out
faults.why: The writer said 'burned out', which means exhausted by work and morale. 'Wore out' is close, but 'the people' for the staff loses the sense that it is our own people.

faults.quote: and it would be a help in getting new hands
faults.why: This is a thin gloss on the hiring point. It lacks Twain's characteristic comic exaggeration, simile or concrete image, so the passage reads as light dialect dressing rather than Twain. There is no humor, irony or deadpan turn.

faults.quote: I know it is a risk, and the customers might not take to it. We could try it for three months, and see.
faults.why: The second paragraph is nearly the writer's own prose with 'clients' swapped for 'customers'. It has no Twain move, and the stiff 'I know it is' sits oddly beside the dialect 'wore out' and 'don't'. The register is inconsistent.

faults.quote: has up and quit
faults.why: This is Huck-style folk vernacular in an office argument. Mixed with 'for the people are' and 'the reports show', the register wavers between Huck and a formal narrator.

faults.quote: The narrator’s aside: “I reckon we ought to cut the week down to four days” — cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 32, ¶ 51
faults.why: This is not an aside. It is the opening claim. The precise chapter and paragraph citations look fabricated and cannot be verified, so they give a false impression of authority.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “for the people are wore out, and the best engineer we had has up and quit.” — cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 3, ¶ 2
faults.why: The sentence is a simple two-clause compound, not a cumulative one. The cited source is dubious.

faults.quote: Deadpan: “The reports show the work don't fall off—it stays the same or goes up” — cites A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 33, ¶ 1
faults.why: Nothing here is deadpan. It is a plain statement, and the citation is not apt. Paragraph 2 has no notes, though it was altered ('customers'), and the notes name nothing that was changed.

faults.quote: he piles the reasons into a spoken run instead of listing them flat
faults.why: The rewrite hardly does this. The reasons are still two clauses plus one more, much as in the draft. The outline claims 'the turn in the last words', but the ending is unchanged and carries no turn. The lesson describes moves the rewrite does not make.

faults.quote: it would be a help in getting new hands; I know it is a risk
faults.why: The outline says the order is changed, with the proposal first and the reasons piled behind it, but the actual order is the writer's own. The outline and rewrite do not match, and no real improvement was made or explained.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and order but is mostly the writer's text with light dialect touches ('reckon', 'wore out', 'up and quit'). It has no real Twain humor or structural move, and the notes cite probably invented chapter and paragraph references and mislabel plain statements as deadpan or cumulative. The teaching claims more than the text delivers.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana called off our dinner, I was not a bit upset—I was relieved, honest—for I had been dreading it the whole week, and I was not proud of it.

I told her it was all right, and we would do it another time, but I did not think we would.

rows.text: When Dana called off our dinner, I was not a bit upset—I was relieved, honest—for I had been dreading it the whole week, and I was not proud of it.

notes.after: When Dana called off our dinner, I was not a bit upset
—I was relieved, honest—
notes.cite: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 26, ¶ 1

notes.after: When Dana called off our dinner, I was not a bit upset—I was relieved, honest—for I had been dreading it the whole week, and I was not proud of it.

rows.text: I told her it was all right, and we would do it another time, but I did not think we would.

notes.after: but I did not think we would.

lessons: Your draft is a straight, short confession in separate little sentences; Twain would let one long sentence gather the news, the relief, and the shame of dreading it, and then drop the polite lie and its flat contradiction at the end. Practise building a run of clauses on and and for that turns once at the end, and never explain the joke.

outline.gist: Dana cancels the dinner; the narrator is not upset.
He is relieved, honestly.
He had dreaded it all week and is not proud of that.
He tells Dana it is fine and they will do it another time.
He does not think they will.

plan.gist: Dana calls off the dinner; the narrator is not a bit upset, is relieved, and confesses he had dreaded it and is not proud.
plan.why: The news comes first, as the writer gave it; then the relief, stated flat; then the confession, all in one run so the confession lands as the turn.

plan.gist: He tells Dana it is all right and they will do it another time, but he does not think they will.
plan.why: The polite answer goes first, and the flat contradiction comes last, so the joke lands where it should and is never explained.

faults.quote: and I was not proud of it
faults.why: The writer's present-tense "I'm not proud of that" is a reflection from now. The rewrite moves it into the past and attaches it to "it", the dinner, so it no longer clearly refers to the relief. The shame loses some force.

faults.quote: but I did not think we would
faults.why: The writer's present-tense "I don't think we will" is a standing, unresolved doubt. Past tense makes it a remembered thought and softens the closing sting.

faults.quote: I was not a bit upset—I was relieved, honest—for I had been dreading it the whole week
faults.why: Apart from "not a bit" and "honest", this is the writer's own sentence with the clauses joined. There is no Twainian specificity, no comic exaggeration, no sly commentary, and no vernacular rhythm. It reads as plain modern prose with small period touches.

faults.quote: I told her it was all right, and we would do it another time, but I did not think we would.
faults.why: This is a near-verbatim restatement. The deadpan turn is the writer's own, and Twain's gift for the dry understatement is not added to.

faults.quote: I was relieved, honest—
faults.why: "Honest" as a bare adverb tacked onto a dash aside reads awkwardly. The doubled "I was" around the dash also feels clumsy, not like a natural Twain aside.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 26, ¶ 41
faults.why: The precise chapter and paragraph citations look unreliable. The phrase "not a bit upset" is not a distinctive move to pin to a particular passage, and Huck Finn ch. 26 is a doubtful match.

faults.quote: [move] The narrator’s aside: “—I was relieved, honest—” — cites A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, ch. 26, ¶ 1
faults.why: The aside is a trivial dash insertion, and the cited source is not clearly apt. The note overstates how Twain-like the change is.

faults.quote: [move] Cumulative sentence
faults.why: The note presents merging the two clauses as a major move. It does not report the tense shifts, which are real changes, and it cites ch. 3 ¶2 as a model without showing the likeness.

faults.quote: Practise building a run of clauses on and and for that turns once at the end
faults.why: The advice is reusable, but the rewrite hardly demonstrates it. Its "and"/"for" chain is just the writer's sentences spliced together, so the writer sees little of how Twain actually makes the turn land.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and the direction of every feeling, but it is a light splice of the original with a few period tags, and the tense shifts blunt the present-tense confession and doubt. The Twain voice is thin, and the notes lean on doubtful pinpoint citations to claim moves that are barely there.
